::: {.atlas-prose}

::: {.atlas-lead}
Every federal law, regulation and guideline the Supreme Court publishes in
consolidated form is one point on this map. Two instruments sit close together
when the texts nearest to their provisions live in the same places — the
organic laws of the public universities, for instance, land beside one
another, whatever words they happen to use.
:::

## How to read the map

::: {.fronts}
::: {.front}
### A point

One law, regulation or guideline. Its area is proportional to its provisions
(articles, transitory articles and the other pieces it is divided into), and
its colour is its collection: blue for laws, green for regulations, magenta
for guidelines.
:::
::: {.front}
### Distance

Two instruments sit together when their provisions' closest texts live in the
same places, not when they use the same words. The map is a picture of where
federal law borrows from and repeats itself.
:::
::: {.front}
### The numbers

Each provision was matched to the single closest text outside its own
instrument. A match shared by *m* instruments gives 1/*m* to each, so every
provision that counts adds up to one. Two kinds of provision are not compared
at all, neither as the provision being matched nor as the text it is matched
to: headings, and transitory provisions, which repeat the standard wording of
a decree. A third kind is matched but not counted: a word-for-word text shared
by several instruments. Of the 161,989 provisions, 28,568 are headings, 21,344
are transitory provisions and 1,715 are word-for-word texts shared by several
instruments, so 110,362 count. Where several regulations or guidelines share a
name, only the most recently issued one is shown: the Supreme Court reissues a
regulation under a new identifier rather than reforming it.
:::
:::

Search for an instrument or click a point: the panel lists the five
instruments its provisions are closest to, with how many of its provisions
went to each, and the five instruments whose provisions point at it hardest.
Lines on the map join it to its five closest instruments, numbered as in the
panel; a name in the panel selects that instrument, so the relations can be
followed from one instrument to the next. Scroll or pinch to zoom, drag to
pan, and press Escape or click an empty spot to clear the selection. The
collection buttons under the map show one collection at a time.

A weight under *Closest instruments* is itself a button: it opens a table of
the provisions behind that number, each beside the closest text the other
instrument has, both in full, with how similar the two are and how much the
match adds to the weight — 1, or 1/*m* when the matching text is shared by *m*
instruments.

## An example

The *LEY que crea la Universidad Autónoma Chapingo* has 28 provisions, 18 of
which count; the other ten are headings and transitory provisions, which are
not compared. For 10 of them, the closest text outside the law belongs to the
*LEY Orgánica de la Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana*; for 7, to the *LEY
Orgánica de la Universidad Autónoma Agraria Antonio Narro*; and the last one
goes to the *LEY Orgánica del Instituto Politécnico Nacional*. On the map the
law sits among the organic laws of the UNAM, Antonio Narro, the UAM and the
IPN. The relation is directed: 24 provisions of other instruments have their
closest text in Chapingo's law, 9 of them in Antonio Narro's and 7 in the
UAM's.

The Constitution has 1,328 provisions, but only its 136 articles and its
preamble are compared, so 137 count. Its closest instrument is the *LEY
General de Instituciones y Procedimientos Electorales*, at 15.0: the table
lists 15 provisions, every one a whole 1, among them articles 41, 51 to 56,
58 to 60 and 63 on elections and Congress. The closest of them, article 96,
is matched to article 494 of that law at a similarity of 0.86, and the
weakest, article 125, to its article 11 at 0.61. The next are the *LEY
Orgánica del Poder Judicial de la Federación* at 9.0 and the *LEY Orgánica del
Congreso General de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos* at 8.0.

## The neighbourhood size

The map is drawn four times from the same data. The neighbourhood size is how
many neighbours each instrument is placed against when the map is drawn: small
values keep tight local groups, such as the universities above, and large
values keep the overall shape, such as how the laws, the regulations and the
guidelines sit relative to one another. Switching it changes the layout, never
the relations the panel lists.

## The similarity

Two provisions are close when the method that compares them says so, and the
map can be drawn from any of three. Two are embedding models of the same
family, which turn each provision into a list of numbers: the 0.6B, which is
the one the map opens on and the one the examples above describe, and the 4B, a
larger model of that family. The third, BM25, is a lexical baseline and not a
model at all: it ranks texts by the words they share, weighting each word by
how rare it is among the provisions being compared, so it knows nothing beyond
the corpus itself and does not match a provision with a differently worded one
that means the same. Its scores are not on a scale from 0 to 1, so the table
behind each weight calls them scores and shows one decimal.

Choosing another method is not a change of view like the neighbourhood size: a
different method finds different closest texts, so the instruments the panel
lists, the weights and the lines change, and the layout is drawn again from
them. The selected instrument stays selected, and the size of the neighbourhood
stays where it was. The map of the 4B or of BM25 is fetched the first time it
is chosen, and the table behind each weight is then read for that method.

::: {.atlas-data}
**Data.** The texts are the three consolidated corpora this project publishes
from the Supreme Court (SCJN) — [laws](leyes.ipynb)
([`scjn-leyes`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-leyes)),
regulations
([`scjn-reglamentos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-reglamentos))
and guidelines
([`scjn-lineamientos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-lineamientos))
— divided into provisions and embedded with `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`, the
map's default, and with `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B`, which the similarity
control switches to, as it does to BM25, a lexical baseline computed from the
same provisions. The map is a UMAP projection, cosine metric, of each instrument's matches. The
Diario Oficial de la Federación remains the official source of legal text.
Map data generated on <span data-atlas-generated>30 September 2026</span>.

*Read more:* how instruments are divided into provisions
([`md2akn`](https://legalia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/md2akn_api.html)) and
how the vectors are read back
([`legalvec`](https://legalia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/legalvec_api.html)).
:::
